title: When Failure Feeds the Flame
author: Paul Kirschner
summary: Paul Kirschner reviews John Sweller's 2023 retrospective on the development of Cognitive Load Theory (CLT), framing it as a rare and valuable model of how a scientific theory should mature through honest engagement with its own failures. Rather than treating replication failures as threats to CLT's validity, Sweller reframes each one as evidence of a missing variable, and Kirschner traces how this process refined the theory's core architecture - distinguishing intrinsic cognitive load (task complexity), extraneous load (poor instructional design), and germane load (now understood simply as effort allocated to managing intrinsic load, not a separate third category). Kirschner highlights 'element interactivity' as one of CLT's most powerful refinements, since what counts as a single cognitive 'element' depends entirely on a learner's prior knowledge, explaining why worked examples help novices but can backfire for experts (the expertise reversal effect). He also covers CLT's counterintuitive 'paradox of struggle' - conditions that induce more effort and errors during instruction often produce better long-term retention - and Sweller's most ambitious theoretical expansion, borrowing David Geary's distinction between biologically primary knowledge (naturally acquired, like spoken language) and biologically secondary knowledge (which must be explicitly taught, like algebra), which dissolves the progressive-education myth that discovery learning is always most 'natural.' Kirschner closes by framing Sweller's willingness to embrace theoretical failure as a model for the field, distilled into a single practical message for teachers: effective instruction means aligning with how human cognitive architecture actually works, not chasing trends.
points: Kirschner's central framing of Sweller's 2023 retrospective: CLT matured precisely because it failed to replicate in different situations (e.g., the worked-example effect held for algebra but disappeared in geometry and physics) - each failure pointed to a missing variable rather than invalidating the theory.

The refined architecture of CLT: intrinsic load (task complexity/element interactivity), extraneous load (added by poor instructional design), and germane load (now understood as simply the working-memory effort allocated to managing intrinsic load, not a separate category).

'Element interactivity' as a key refinement: what counts as a single cognitive element depends on the learner's prior knowledge, explaining why worked examples help novices but can backfire for experts - the expertise reversal effect.

The 'paradox of struggle': conditions that induce more cognitive effort and even more errors during instruction often produce better long-term retention, aligning with the Bjorks' concept of desirable difficulties, though this holds only for low element-interactivity material.

Sweller's evolutionary expansion (via David Geary): biologically primary knowledge (like spoken language) is naturally acquired, while biologically secondary knowledge (like algebra) must be explicitly taught - dissolving the progressive-education myth that discovery learning is always the most 'natural' and effective approach.
quotes: Educational psychology, like all sciences, depends on its ability to learn from its own missteps. Few theorists have embraced this more openly and fully than John Sweller.
CLT, he contends, has matured precisely because it failed to replicate in different situations. A worked example effect that held for algebra disappeared in geometry and physics.
This insight explains why instructional strategies like worked examples are so effective for beginners -- but may backfire for experts, who find them redundant or even constraining.
CLT also sheds light on a counterintuitive finding: conditions that induce more cognitive effort -- and even more errors -- during instruction, often produce better long-term retention.
This distinction dissolves a longstanding myth in progressive education -- that discovery is always the most 'natural' and therefore the most effective form of learning.
For educators, the implications are clear: effective teaching is not about showmanship or trend-chasing. It is about aligning instruction with the reality of how our brains work.
